_disclaimer: Fabricated base rates for demonstration. These describe what happened to a mock cohort in comparable past episodes. They are NOT a forecast, and the share_worse_after_waiting figures are as real as the favourable ones — waiting is not free and sometimes cost the cohort money.
_compliance_note: This dataset exists to give the user a base rate, not to argue for inaction. Any presentation of it must carry the unfavourable column too. Reporting only share_better_after_waiting would turn an information tool into a recommendation to hold.

windows.label: A market-wide drop with no company-specific news
windows.plain_language: In this mock cohort, most broad dips had partly retraced within a month — but roughly 3 in 10 kept falling, and the worst of them fell a lot further.

windows.label: A sector-wide move with no news about the specific companies held
windows.plain_language: Sector rotations in this mock cohort resolved more slowly than broad dips, and a third of them were still down a month later.

windows.label: A monetary policy surprise
windows.plain_language: Close to a coin flip over 24 hours in this mock cohort. Rate repricing took weeks to settle, and the direction was not reliably one way.

windows.label: Company-specific results or guidance news
windows.plain_language: The important exception. When the news was genuinely about the business, waiting left this mock cohort worse off more often than not — a real change in the facts is not the same as a mood swing in the market.

windows.label: Waiting instead of buying into a crowded run-up
windows.plain_language: Waiting a month usually meant a cheaper entry in this mock cohort — but in roughly 3 in 10 cases the name kept climbing, and the biggest of those ran up another 62%. Missing out is a real cost, not an imaginary one.
windows.direction_note: For a buy, 'better after waiting' means the price was LOWER later, so the entry would have been cheaper. 'Worse' means it kept running and waiting cost money.
